chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ahmad ibn al-Walid (may God be pleased with him) narrated that Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated from Ahmad and Abdullah, sons of Muhammad ibn Isa, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad ibn Uthman al-Nabbal, from Ubaydullah ibn Ali al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

he mentioned that Barira was with a husband of hers while she was a slave. Aisha bought her and freed her. The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) gave her the choice: if she wished, she could stay with her husband, and if she wished, she could leave him. Her former masters, who had sold her, had stipulated with Aisha that they would have her manumission right (walā'). The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'The manumission right belongs to the one who freed her.' Meat was given in charity to Barira, and she presented it to the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family). Aisha hung it up and said: 'Indeed, the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) does not eat charity (sadaqah).' When the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) came and saw the meat hanging, he said: 'What is the matter with this meat? It has not been cooked.' She said: 'O Messenger of God, it was given in charity to Barira and she presented it to us, and you do not eat charity.' He said: 'It is charity for her and a gift for us.' Then he ordered it to be cooked, and three traditions were established through this incident.

key_terms.بَرِيرَة: Barira, a freed slave woman whose case is central to this narration.
key_terms.خِيَار: Option or choice, specifically the right to choose to stay in or leave a marriage contract.
key_terms.صَدَقَة: Charity given to the poor, which the Prophet generally did not consume personally.
key_terms.هَدِيَّة: Gift, which the Prophet could consume, distinguishing it from charity.
key_terms.وَلَاء: Manumission right; the right of the former master or his heirs to inherit from a freed slave or be inherited by them.

ai.seo_question: What are the three legal traditions established by the Prophet through the case of Barira?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Khisal elucidates three foundational legal principles (sunan) through the narrative of Barira, emphasizing the Prophet's authority to override customary stipulations regarding walā' (manumission right) in favor of the actual manumitter. It further clarifies the jurisprudential distinction between sadaqah (charity) and hadiyyah (gift), demonstrating how the Prophet could consume the former while giving the latter, thereby resolving the concern of his status regarding impurities. The narration also establishes the right of option (khiyār) for a freed slave woman, highlighting the flexibility in marital bonds upon manumission.
